name: Kabir
role: Weaver-poet of Varanasi and sant of north India
summary: Kabir was a 15th-century poet-saint of Varanasi whose short, plain couplets urged people to look inward. Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs all honour his verses.
about: Kabir is traditionally said to have been born in Varanasi and to have lived as a weaver. Scholars disagree on when: some propose 1398 to 1448, others 1440 to 1518. His poems used a mixed everyday language and came to be known as bani, with short couplets called dohas or sakhis. Many were passed on by singing for about two centuries before being written down, so later hands added and changed verses. Kabir spoke of a God beyond any single name or temple, and he often questioned rituals, pride and sectarian quarrels. Tradition links him with the teacher Ramananda. Both Hindus and Muslims claimed him after his death. His verses appear in the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, and in the Bijak, the book of the Kabir panth, a community that honours him as its founder.
kidSummary: Kabir was a weaver who wrote short, clear poems that made people think. He said that God is not found only in one temple or mosque, but in a kind and honest heart. People of many faiths still sing his couplets today.

story.title: A weaver's home
story.text: Kabir is said to have lived in Varanasi and worked as a weaver. One tradition says a Muslim weaver couple, Niru and Nima, raised him.

story.title: Songs, not sermons
story.text: He spoke in simple everyday words and short verses, so that everyone could understand them and sing them.

story.title: A guru for a weaver's boy
story.text: A legend says that as a small boy Kabir claimed Ramananda as his teacher, though he was a weaver's child. The story says Ramananda gave up untouchability.

story.title: Questioning pride
story.text: Kabir asked why people fought over names for God or over who was high or low. He pointed people back to honesty and love.

story.title: Friends and critics
story.text: His straight talk pleased many and angered others, and in his life both Hindus and Muslims are said to have been upset with him.

story.title: Claimed by all
story.text: A popular belief says Kabir died at Maghar, not Kashi, and only flowers lay where he rested. Hindus and Muslims who loved him shared them.

teaches: Look inward instead of arguing over outward differences
Humility and the dropping of pride
emblems: Kanthi mala (tulsi bead necklace) among followers

facts.text: Some followers believe Kabir appeared on a lotus in the Lahartara pond rather than being born. Another account says Muslim weavers Niru and Nima found and raised him there.
One of Kabir's best-known couplets says that he set out to find a bad person and found none. When he looked inside himself, he found no one worse than himself.
His poems blend Khadi boli, Braj, Bhojpuri, Marwari and Awadhi. That is why the language is called Panchmel Khichri, a five-mix hotchpotch, like a pot of mixed rice and lentils.
The Sikh scripture holds Kabir's verses, and he is its largest contributor from outside the Sikh Gurus. Sikhs call him Bhagat Kabir.
Varanasi has two temples honouring Kabir, one run by Hindus and one by Muslims, and both sing his songs every day.
Hindu Kabir panth followers call God Raam, while Muslim followers use the name Khuda, so the panth welcomes people of both faiths.

A popular belief says that when Kabir passed away at Maghar, only fragrant flowers were found where his body lay. Hindu and Muslim followers shared them, and built a samadhi and a dargah about 100 metres apart.
Tradition says Kabir chose to die at Maghar rather than Kashi, to break the belief that anyone dying in Maghar would be reborn as a donkey. A fair is held there every year on Makar Sankranti.
A legend says that as a boy of about five, Kabir claimed Ramananda as his guru despite being from a low-caste weaver family. Ramananda is said to have given up untouchability after this meeting.
Tagore's English Songs of Kabir was first printed in 1915. The critic V. C. Mishra has suggested that only six of its hundred poems are truly Kabir's.
Kabir's own verses suggest he welcomed his critics. He called the slanderer a friend, because the slander brought him closer to God.
Kabir urged people to look inside their own heart, where he said both Karim and Ram can be found. He also teased that the whole world died reading book after book.
Legends make Kabir an underdog who passes every trial set by a sultan, a Brahmin, a qazi, a merchant, a god and a goddess. Many scholars doubt these tales as history.
Dharamdas, a chief disciple, spread Kabir's teachings. Kabir is said to have blessed his line to last 42 generations, and the Dharamdasi centre is in Chhattisgarh.
Kabir and his followers called his spoken poems banis, or utterances. Couplets are called dohe or sakhi, and sakhi means 'witness', as if each verse gives testimony about the truth.
In Varanasi, a locality called Kabir Chaura is where his family is believed to have lived. A Kabir math there celebrates his life, and a house called Niru Tila holds the graves of Niru and Nima.
Scholar Linda Hess warns that picturing Kabir as a simple blend of Hinduism and Islam is misleading. She says he declared his independence from both and attacked what he saw as follies in each.
The Kabir panth took shape in the 1600s and 1700s, long after Kabir. Its followers are now estimated at about 9.6 million, up from about 843,000 in the 1901 census.
Kabir's verses are found in more than one scripture: the Sikh Guru Granth Sahib, Garib Das's Satguru Granth Sahib and Dharamdas's Kabir Sagar all include them.
A 1907 study by G. H. Westcott noted 82 works attributed to Kabir. His poems were sung from memory for about two centuries before the Bijak was first written down in the 1600s.
Scholars disagree on how close Guru Nanak was to Kabir's Sant tradition. Hew McLeod placed Nanak within it, while J. S. Grewal argued McLeod stressed ideas and overlooked differences in practice.

quiz.why: Kabir is said to have been a weaver.

quiz.q: Which scripture includes verses by Kabir?
quiz.why: His verses are part of the Sikh scripture.

quiz.q: What does the word sakhi mean?
Which poet translated Kabir's songs into English in a famous book?
Where is Kabir said to have died?
quiz.why: His traditional resting place is Maghar.
